item.title: CSS Introduction
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
HTML gives a page its structure: headings, paragraphs, lists, forms. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how that structure looks: colours, fonts, spacing, layout, even animations. Every good-looking website you've ever used is HTML plus CSS.

Before and after CSS

Here is a small page with no CSS at all:

<h1>VitalStack</h1>
<p>Learn to code, one lesson at a time.</p>
<a href="#">Start learning</a>

It works, but it looks plain. Now the same HTML with a few lines of CSS:

<style>
  body {
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
    background: #f5f7fb;
    padding: 32px;
  }
  h1 {
    color: #2563eb;
  }
  a {
    display: inline-block;
    background: #2563eb;
    color: white;
    padding: 10px 18px;
    border-radius: 8px;
    text-decoration: none;
  }
</style>

<h1>VitalStack</h1>
<p>Learn to code, one lesson at a time.</p>
<a href="#">Start learning</a>

Open it with Try it Yourself. The HTML didn't change at all; CSS changed the font, the background, the heading colour, and turned a plain link into a button.

Anatomy of a CSS rule

h1 {
  color: #2563eb;
  font-size: 32px;
}
  • h1 is the selector: which elements the rule applies to.
  • Everything inside { } is the declaration block.
  • color: #2563eb; is a declaration, made of a property (color) and a value (#2563eb), separated by a colon and ending with a semicolon.

A rule can have as many declarations as you like. Put each on its own line to keep it readable.

What "cascading" means

Several rules can apply to the same element. The cascade is the set of rules that decides which one wins. In short:

  1. More specific selectors beat less specific ones (an id beats a class, a class beats an element name).
  2. If two rules are equally specific, the one that comes later wins.
<style>
  p { color: gray; }
  p { color: green; }
</style>
<p>What colour am I?</p>

The paragraph is green, because the second rule comes later. You'll learn the full details in the Selectors lesson.

Inheritance

Some properties, mainly text-related ones like color, font-family and line-height, are inherited: children take them from their parent. That's why setting a font on body changes the font of the whole page. Box-related properties such as border, padding and background are not inherited.

Why keep style separate from HTML

You *could* style every element with a style attribute, but separating CSS from HTML has big advantages:

  • Change once, update everywhere. One stylesheet can style hundreds of pages. Change a colour in one place and the whole site updates.
  • Cleaner HTML that only describes content.
  • Faster sites: the browser downloads the stylesheet once and caches it.
  • Different looks for different devices (phone, desktop, print) from the same HTML.

CSS comments

/* Main heading colour */
h1 {
  color: #2563eb; /* brand blue */
}

Comments start with /* and end with */. CSS has no // single-line comments.

Common mistakes

  • Missing semicolons. color: red font-size: 20px; breaks both declarations. End every declaration with ;.
  • Missing closing brace }, which can break every rule after it.
  • Spelling property names wrong (colour instead of color). The browser silently ignores properties it doesn't know.
  • Spaces in values where they don't belong, like 20 px. Write 20px.

Exercise

Open the "after" example with Try it Yourself and:

  1. Change the heading colour to any colour you like.
  2. Change the background of the page to white.
  3. Make the button's corners fully round with border-radius: 999px;.
  4. Add a rule for p that sets font-size: 18px; and color: #444;.

Summary

  • CSS controls how HTML looks: colours, fonts, spacing and layout.
  • A rule = selector + declaration block; a declaration = property + value.
  • The cascade decides which rule wins; some properties are inherited.
  • Keeping CSS separate from HTML makes sites easier to change and faster.

Next, you'll learn the three ways to add CSS to a page.
item.excerpt:encoded: What CSS is, how a CSS rule is built from a selector and declarations, and why separating style from HTML makes websites easier to build and change.

item.title: How to Add CSS
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
There are three places you can write CSS: directly on an element, in a <style> element inside the page, or in a separate .css file. Real websites mostly use the third, but you'll meet all three.

1. Inline styles

Add a style attribute to one element:

<p style="color: crimson; font-weight: bold;">This paragraph is styled inline.</p>
<p>This one isn't.</p>

Inline styles affect only that one element. They're handy for a quick test, or when a script changes one element's style, but they have big downsides:

  • You can't reuse them; every element needs its own copy.
  • They mix content and design, making HTML hard to read.
  • They're very hard to override from a stylesheet.

2. Internal stylesheet

Put rules inside a <style> element, usually in the <head>:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>Internal CSS</title>
  <style>
    body { font-family: Georgia, serif; }
    h1 { color: teal; }
    p { line-height: 1.6; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Internal stylesheet</h1>
  <p>Every paragraph on this page gets the same line height.</p>
  <p>Including this one.</p>
</body>
</html>

The rules apply to the whole page. This is fine for a single-page project, an email template or a quick demo (the examples in these lessons use it so they run in Try it Yourself). But the styles can't be shared with other pages.

3. External stylesheet (the normal way)

Write the CSS in its own file, for example styles.css:

/* styles.css */
body {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  margin: 0;
}
h1 {
  color: #2563eb;
}

Then link it from the <head> of every page:

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My site</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
  • rel="stylesheet" says what kind of file it is.
  • href is the path to the file, relative or absolute, just like a link.

Benefits:

  • One file styles the whole site. Change it once and every page updates.
  • Faster: the browser downloads styles.css once and reuses it from its cache on every other page.
  • Clean HTML with no styling mixed in.

A typical project folder looks like this:

my-site/
├── index.html
├── about.html
└── css/
    └── styles.css

With that structure, the link is <link rel="stylesheet" href="css/styles.css">.

Several stylesheets

You can link more than one file. They're applied in order, so later files can override earlier ones:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/base.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/theme.css">

Many sites also load web fonts this way, for example a stylesheet from Google Fonts.

Which one wins?

When the same property is set in more than one place for the same element and with equal selector strength, the order decides:

  1. Browser default styles (weakest)
  2. External and internal stylesheets, in the order they appear in the page
  3. Inline style attributes (strongest)
<style>
  p { color: blue; }
</style>
<p style="color: green;">I'm green: the inline style wins.</p>
<p>I'm blue.</p>

There's also !important, which forces a declaration to win (color: red !important;). Avoid it: it makes CSS very hard to manage, because the only way to beat it is another !important.

When to use which

Common mistakes

  • **Wrong path in href**, so the stylesheet never loads and the page looks unstyled. Check the browser's developer tools (F12 → Network) for a red 404.
  • **Writing <style> tags inside a .css file.** A CSS file contains only CSS.
  • **Using <link> in the body.** Put stylesheets in the <head> so the page doesn't flash unstyled.
  • **Overusing !important.**

Exercise

  1. Create a folder with index.html and css/styles.css on your computer.
  2. Link the stylesheet and set a background colour on body and a colour on h1.
  3. Create about.html, link the same stylesheet, and check both pages share the design.
  4. Add an inline style to one paragraph and confirm it beats the stylesheet.

Summary

  • CSS can be inline (style attribute), internal (<style>) or external (<link> to a .css file).
  • External stylesheets are the standard for real websites.
  • Later rules beat earlier ones; inline styles beat stylesheets; avoid !important.

Next, you'll learn how selectors choose which elements a rule styles.

item.title: CSS Selectors
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A selector is the part of a CSS rule that chooses which elements to style. Learning selectors well is the key to writing short, clean CSS. This lesson covers the selectors you'll use every day and the rule that settles conflicts: specificity.

Basic selectors

<style>
  p { color: #444; }                 /* element (type) selector */
  .highlight { background: #fff3b0; } /* class selector */
  #intro { font-size: 20px; }        /* id selector */
  * { box-sizing: border-box; }      /* universal selector: every element */
</style>

<p id="intro">This is the introduction.</p>
<p>A normal paragraph with a <span class="highlight">highlighted phrase</span>.</p>
<p class="highlight">A whole highlighted paragraph.</p>
  • Element: p matches every <p>.
  • Class: .highlight matches every element with class="highlight".
  • Id: #intro matches the one element with id="intro".
  • Universal: * matches everything.

You can combine an element and a class with no space: p.highlight matches only paragraphs that have the class.

Grouping selectors

Separate selectors with commas to give them the same styles:

h1, h2, h3 {
  font-family: Georgia, serif;
  color: #1e293b;
}

Combinators: selecting by position

<style>
  article p { color: green; }      /* descendant: any p inside article */
  ul > li { font-weight: bold; }   /* child: only direct li children of ul */
  h2 + p { font-style: italic; }   /* adjacent sibling: the p right after an h2 */
</style>

<article>
  <h2>Article title</h2>
  <p>First paragraph (green and italic).</p>
  <p>Second paragraph (green only).</p>
</article>

<ul>
  <li>Direct child (bold)
    <ol><li>Nested item: not a direct child of ul, so its text isn't bold</li></ol>
  </li>
</ul>
  • A B (space): B anywhere inside A.
  • A > B: B directly inside A.
  • A + B: B immediately after A, with the same parent.
  • A ~ B: any B after A with the same parent.

Note: the nested item's text is still bold because font-weight is inherited from its parent <li>; the selector itself didn't match it.

Attribute selectors

a[target="_blank"] { color: purple; }     /* exact value */
input[type="email"] { border-color: blue; }
a[href^="https"] { font-weight: bold; }   /* value starts with */
a[href$=".pdf"] { color: crimson; }       /* value ends with */

These are great for forms and for styling links by their destination.

Pseudo-classes: state and position

A pseudo-class starts with a colon and selects elements in a certain state or position:

<style>
  a:hover { color: crimson; }
  button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid orange; }
  input:invalid { border: 2px solid red; }
  li:first-child { color: green; }
  li:last-child { color: blue; }
  li:nth-child(even) { background: #f1f5f9; }
  p:not(.note) { color: #555; }
</style>

<a href="#">Hover over me</a>
<p><button>Tab to me</button></p>
<p><input type="email" placeholder="Type an invalid email"></p>
<ul>
  <li>First</li><li>Second</li><li>Third</li><li>Fourth</li>
</ul>
<p class="note">A note</p>
<p>Not a note</p>

:nth-child(even) (or odd, 3, 3n) is perfect for striped table rows. :not() excludes elements.

Pseudo-elements

A pseudo-element starts with two colons and styles a part of an element:

p::first-line { font-weight: bold; }
.required::after { content: " *"; color: red; }
::selection { background: #2563eb; color: white; }

::before and ::after insert decorative content. They need the content property, even if it's empty (content: "").

Specificity: which rule wins

When two rules conflict, the more specific selector wins, no matter which comes first. Think of it as a score with three columns:

Compare from the left: one id beats any number of classes, and one class beats any number of elements. If the scores are equal, the later rule wins. Inline styles beat all of these.

<style>
  #title { color: blue; }
  .heading { color: green; }
  h1 { color: red; }
</style>
<h1 id="title" class="heading">I'm blue: the id is most specific</h1>

Practical advice: style with classes, keep selectors short, and avoid ids in CSS. Low, even specificity makes your CSS predictable.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the dot or hash: highlight { } looks for a <highlight> element.
  • Adding a space by accident: p .note (note inside p) is not p.note (p that has class note).
  • Long chains like body div.main ul li a, which are fragile and hard to override.
  • **Fighting specificity with !important** instead of simplifying selectors.

Exercise

  1. Make every second row of a list grey with :nth-child(even).
  2. Colour links that open in a new tab differently with an attribute selector.
  3. Add a red asterisk after every label with class required using ::after.
  4. Write two conflicting rules and predict which wins, then test it.

Summary

  • Element, .class, #id and * are the basic selectors; commas group them.
  • Combinators (space, >, +, ~) select by position.
  • Pseudo-classes (:hover, :nth-child) select by state; pseudo-elements (::before) style parts.
  • Specificity decides conflicts: ids > classes > elements; then the later rule wins.

Next, you'll learn all the ways to write colours in CSS.

item.title: CSS Colors
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Colour is one of the first things people notice about a website. CSS gives you several ways to write the same colour, and knowing them all makes it easy to copy colours from design tools and adjust them.

Where colours are used

<style>
  .demo {
    color: white;              /* text colour */
    background-color: #2563eb; /* background */
    border: 4px solid #1e40af; /* border colour */
    padding: 16px;
  }
</style>
<div class="demo">Text, background and border colours</div>

color always means the text colour. Backgrounds and borders have their own properties.

Colour names

p { color: tomato; }
h1 { color: navy; }

CSS knows about 140 names like red, teal, gold, slategray and rebeccapurple. They're easy to read but limited, so real designs use the formats below.

Hex codes

h1 { color: #2563eb; }
p  { color: #333; }   /* short form of #333333 */

A hex colour is # followed by three pairs of hexadecimal digits (0–9, a–f) for red, green and blue. 00 means none of that colour; ff means full.

  • #000000 is black, #ffffff is white.
  • #ff0000 is pure red, #00ff00 green, #0000ff blue.
  • If each pair has two equal digits, you can shorten it: #336699 → #369.

Hex is the format you'll copy most often from design tools like Figma.

rgb()

h1 { color: rgb(37, 99, 235); }

The same red-green-blue idea, with numbers from 0 to 255. rgb(37, 99, 235) is exactly the same colour as #2563eb.

hsl(): the most human-friendly format

.primary { color: hsl(221, 83%, 53%); }
  • Hue (0–360): the position on the colour wheel. 0 is red, 120 green, 240 blue.
  • Saturation (0–100%): from grey to full colour.
  • Lightness (0–100%): 0% is black, 50% normal, 100% white.

HSL makes it easy to create shades of one colour: keep the hue, change the lightness.

<style>
  .shade { padding: 10px; color: white; }
  .s1 { background: hsl(221, 83%, 30%); }
  .s2 { background: hsl(221, 83%, 45%); }
  .s3 { background: hsl(221, 83%, 60%); }
  .s4 { background: hsl(221, 83%, 75%); color: #111; }
</style>
<div class="shade s1">Dark</div>
<div class="shade s2">Medium</div>
<div class="shade s3">Light</div>
<div class="shade s4">Lighter</div>

Transparency

Add a fourth value for alpha (opacity), from 0 (invisible) to 1 (solid):

<style>
  .photo {
    background: url("https://picsum.photos/id/1018/400/200") center/cover;
    height: 200px;
    display: flex;
    align-items: end;
  }
  .caption {
    background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.6);
    color: white;
    padding: 12px;
    width: 100%;
  }
</style>
<div class="photo"><div class="caption">A dark see-through caption over a photo</div></div>

You can write transparency as rgb(0 0 0 / 0.6), rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6), hsl(221 83% 53% / 0.5) or an 8-digit hex like #2563eb80. They all work in modern browsers.

There's also the opacity property, but it makes the whole element see-through, including its text. To fade only a background, use a transparent colour instead.

currentColor and transparent

  • transparent is fully see-through.
  • currentColor means "the current text colour". It's useful for borders and icons that should match the text: border: 2px solid currentColor;.

Choosing a palette

Most good websites use very few colours:

  • One brand colour for links, buttons and highlights.
  • Neutrals (near-black, greys, off-white) for text and backgrounds.
  • Status colours: green for success, red for errors, yellow/orange for warnings.

Use pure black (#000) for text sparingly; a very dark grey like #1f2937 is softer to read.

Contrast matters

Text must stand out from its background. The accessibility guideline (WCAG) asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Light grey text on white often fails. In Chrome or Firefox, open developer tools (F12), click a text element's colour swatch, and the colour picker shows the contrast ratio.

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting the #** in hex codes: color: 2563eb; is ignored.
  • Low-contrast text, like #aaa on white.
  • **Using opacity to fade a background**, which fades the text too.
  • Too many colours. Pick a small palette and reuse it.

Exercise

  1. Write the same colour as a name, hex, rgb and hsl and put four boxes side by side to compare.
  2. Create five shades of green by changing only the lightness in hsl().
  3. Add a semi-transparent caption over an image.
  4. Check the contrast of your text with your browser's developer tools.

Summary

  • color is text colour; background-color and border-color are separate.
  • Write colours as names, hex (#2563eb), rgb() or hsl().
  • Add alpha for transparency; opacity fades the whole element.
  • Use a small palette and keep text contrast at 4.5:1 or higher.

Next, you'll style backgrounds with colours, images and gradients.
item.excerpt:encoded: Colour names, hex codes, rgb, hsl and transparency, how to pick a small colour palette, and how to check text contrast.

item.title: CSS Backgrounds
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Backgrounds turn plain boxes into banners, cards and sections. In this lesson you'll use colours, images and gradients as backgrounds and control exactly how images are sized and placed.

Background colour

<style>
  .box { background-color: #e0f2fe; padding: 20px; }
</style>
<div class="box">A light blue box</div>

Background images

<style>
  .pattern {
    background-image: url("https://picsum.photos/id/1080/120/120");
    height: 240px;
  }
</style>
<div class="pattern"></div>

url() takes the path to the image. By default the image repeats in both directions to fill the box. That's useful for patterns but usually not what you want for photos.

Unlike <img>, a background image has no alt text and is invisible to screen readers. Use backgrounds only for decoration; if the image matters to the content, use an <img> element.

background-repeat

.a { background-repeat: no-repeat; } /* show it once */
.b { background-repeat: repeat-x; }  /* only horizontally */
.c { background-repeat: repeat-y; }  /* only vertically */

background-position

.hero { background-position: center; }
.logo-corner { background-position: right bottom; }
.custom { background-position: 20px 40px; }  /* x then y */

You can use keywords (top, bottom, left, right, center), lengths or percentages.

background-size: cover and contain

This is the property you'll use most:

<style>
  .frame {
    width: 260px;
    height: 160px;
    border: 2px solid #94a3b8;
    margin-bottom: 12px;
    background: url("https://picsum.photos/id/1015/600/300") no-repeat center #f1f5f9;
  }
  .cover { background-size: cover; }
  .contain { background-size: contain; }
</style>
<div class="frame cover"></div>
<div class="frame contain"></div>
  • cover scales the image to fill the whole box, cropping the edges if needed. Perfect for hero banners.
  • contain scales it to fit inside the box completely, which can leave empty space.
  • You can also give exact sizes: background-size: 100px auto;.

Gradients

Gradients are backgrounds made by CSS itself, so they need no image file:

<style>
  .g { height: 80px; margin-bottom: 10px; border-radius: 8px; }
  .g1 { background: linear-gradient(#2563eb, #7c3aed); }
  .g2 { background: linear-gradient(to right, #f97316, #facc15); }
  .g3 { background: linear-gradient(135deg, #10b981 0%, #3b82f6 50%, #8b5cf6 100%); }
  .g4 { background: radial-gradient(circle, #fde68a, #f59e0b); }
</style>
<div class="g g1"></div>
<div class="g g2"></div>
<div class="g g3"></div>
<div class="g g4"></div>
  • linear-gradient(direction, colour1, colour2, ...) blends in a straight line. The direction can be to right, to bottom left or an angle like 135deg.
  • Percentages after colours (colour stops) control where each colour sits.
  • radial-gradient() blends outward from a centre.

Several backgrounds at once

You can layer backgrounds, separated by commas. The first one is on top. A common trick is a dark gradient over a photo so white text stays readable:

<style>
  .hero {
    background:
      linear-gradient(rgb(0 0 0 / 0.55), rgb(0 0 0 / 0.55)),
      url("https://picsum.photos/id/1044/900/400") center / cover no-repeat;
    color: white;
    padding: 80px 24px;
    text-align: center;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .hero h1 { margin: 0 0 8px; }
</style>
<section class="hero">
  <h1>Learn to code for free</h1>
  <p>Short lessons, real examples, no sign-up needed.</p>
</section>

The background shorthand

All background properties can be set in one line:

.hero {
  background: #1e293b url("hero.jpg") center / cover no-repeat;
}

The order is flexible, but the size must come straight after the position, separated by /. Any part you leave out goes back to its default, which can accidentally reset something you set earlier.

background-attachment

background-attachment: fixed; keeps the image still while the page scrolls (a "parallax" feel). It's often ignored on phones and can make scrolling slow, so use it sparingly.

Common mistakes

  • **Wrong image path in url(). Paths in a CSS file are relative to the CSS file**, not the HTML page.
  • Forgetting the box needs a height. An empty div with a background image has zero height and shows nothing.
  • White text on a busy photo without a dark overlay.
  • Important images as backgrounds, which screen readers can't see.

Exercise

  1. Create a 300 × 200 box with a photo background using cover.
  2. Add a gradient overlay and white centred text on top.
  3. Make a striped button with linear-gradient(to right, ...).
  4. Try contain instead of cover and note the difference.

Summary

  • background-color, background-image, -repeat, -position and -size control backgrounds.
  • cover fills and crops; contain fits without cropping.
  • linear-gradient() and radial-gradient() create backgrounds with no image file.
  • Layer a gradient over a photo to keep text readable.

Next, you'll draw borders, rounded corners and shadows.
