item.title: CSS Borders
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Borders draw lines around elements. Together with rounded corners and shadows, they're how you make cards, buttons, inputs and avatars look finished.

The three parts of a border

<style>
  .b {
    border-width: 3px;
    border-style: solid;
    border-color: #2563eb;
    padding: 12px;
  }
</style>
<p class="b">A 3px solid blue border.</p>

A border needs a style to appear. Without border-style, there's no border at all, even if you set a width and colour.

Border styles

<style>
  .s { border-width: 4px; border-color: #334155; padding: 8px; margin: 8px 0; }
</style>
<p class="s" style="border-style: solid;">solid</p>
<p class="s" style="border-style: dashed;">dashed</p>
<p class="s" style="border-style: dotted;">dotted</p>
<p class="s" style="border-style: double;">double</p>
<p class="s" style="border-style: groove;">groove</p>
<p class="s" style="border-style: none;">none</p>

In real designs you'll use solid 95% of the time, and occasionally dashed for things like "drop a file here" areas.

The border shorthand

Write all three parts on one line, in any order:

.card { border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; }

This is how you'll almost always write borders.

Individual sides

<style>
  .note {
    border-left: 5px solid #f59e0b;
    background: #fffbeb;
    padding: 12px 16px;
  }
  .title {
    border-bottom: 2px solid #2563eb;
    padding-bottom: 6px;
  }
</style>
<h2 class="title">Section title with an underline</h2>
<p class="note">A note with a coloured bar on the left.</p>

Use border-top, border-right, border-bottom and border-left to style one side. A left border on a tinted box is a classic "note" or "tip" style.

Rounded corners with border-radius

<style>
  .r { background: #dbeafe; padding: 16px; margin-bottom: 10px; }
  .r1 { border-radius: 6px; }
  .r2 { border-radius: 20px; }
  .r3 { border-radius: 999px; text-align: center; }
  .r4 { border-radius: 20px 0 20px 0; }
</style>
<div class="r r1">Slightly rounded (6px)</div>
<div class="r r2">Very rounded (20px)</div>
<div class="r r3">Pill shape (999px)</div>
<div class="r r4">Opposite corners only</div>
  • One value rounds all four corners.
  • Four values go clockwise from the top-left: top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left.
  • A very large value like 999px makes a "pill", perfect for tags and buttons.

border-radius works even without a border: it rounds the background too.

Circles

A square with border-radius: 50% becomes a circle:

<style>
  .avatar {
    width: 120px;
    height: 120px;
    border-radius: 50%;
    object-fit: cover;
    border: 4px solid white;
    box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.25);
  }
</style>
<img class="avatar" src="https://picsum.photos/id/64/240/240" alt="Profile photo">

object-fit: cover stops the photo from being squashed if it isn't square.

Box shadows

<style>
  .card {
    max-width: 280px;
    padding: 20px;
    border-radius: 12px;
    background: white;
    box-shadow: 0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.12);
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  body { background: #f1f5f9; padding: 24px; }
</style>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Card title</h3>
  <p>A soft shadow makes the card float above the page.</p>
</div>

box-shadow: x-offset y-offset blur colour;

  • Positive x moves the shadow right; positive y moves it down.
  • A bigger blur makes it softer.
  • Use a transparent black for natural shadows. Strong, dark shadows look dated.
  • Add a fourth length for spread, and the keyword inset for an inner shadow.

Outline: a border that takes no space

button:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #f59e0b;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

An outline looks like a border but doesn't take up space and doesn't move anything. Browsers use it to show keyboard focus. If you restyle focus, use outline, never just remove it.

Common mistakes

  • No border-style, so the border never appears.
  • **border-radius: 50% on a rectangle**, which makes an oval, not a circle. Make width and height equal first.
  • Heavy shadows like 5px 5px 5px black. Keep shadows soft and subtle.
  • Removing focus outlines with outline: none and nothing in their place.

Exercise

  1. Style a "warning" box with a thick orange left border and a pale orange background.
  2. Make a pill-shaped tag that says "Beginner".
  3. Turn a photo into a round avatar with a white border and soft shadow.
  4. Build a card with rounded corners and a subtle shadow, and give it a bigger shadow on hover with .card:hover.

Summary

  • A border needs width, style and colour; the border shorthand sets all three.
  • border-top, -right, -bottom, -left style one side.
  • border-radius rounds corners; 50% on a square makes a circle.
  • box-shadow adds depth; outline is for focus and takes no space.

Next, you'll control the space around and inside elements with margin and padding.
item.excerpt:encoded: Border width, style and colour, single sides, the border shorthand, rounded corners with border-radius, circles, outlines and box shadows.

item.title: CSS Margin and Padding
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Good spacing is the secret behind clean designs. CSS has two spacing properties: padding adds space *inside* an element, between its content and its border; margin adds space *outside*, between the element and its neighbours.

Padding vs margin

<style>
  .box {
    background: #dbeafe;
    border: 2px solid #2563eb;
    padding: 20px;  /* inside the border */
    margin: 30px;   /* outside the border */
  }
  body { background: #fef3c7; }
</style>
<div class="box">Padding pushes the border away from this text. Margin pushes other things away from the border.</div>
<div class="box">A second box.</div>

Look at it with Try it Yourself: the blue background fills the padding area, but the margin is transparent (you see the yellow page through it).

A simple way to remember:

  • Padding = cushion inside the box. Background colour shows in it.
  • Margin = gap outside the box. Always transparent.

One to four values

Both properties accept one to four values. They go clockwise from the top:

padding: 10px;                 /* all four sides */
padding: 10px 20px;            /* top & bottom 10px, left & right 20px */
padding: 10px 20px 30px;       /* top 10, left & right 20, bottom 30 */
padding: 10px 20px 30px 40px;  /* top, right, bottom, left */

Think of a clock: Top, Right, Bottom, Left ("TRouBLe" helps some people remember).

You can also set one side at a time:

margin-top: 0;
margin-bottom: 24px;
padding-left: 16px;

Buttons: padding in practice

<style>
  .btn {
    background: #2563eb;
    color: white;
    border: none;
    border-radius: 8px;
    font-size: 16px;
    padding: 12px 24px;
  }
  .btn-small { padding: 6px 12px; font-size: 14px; }
</style>
<button class="btn">Normal button</button>
<button class="btn btn-small">Small button</button>

More horizontal than vertical padding is what makes a button look like a button.

Centring a block with margin: auto

A block with a fixed width can be centred horizontally with auto left and right margins:

<style>
  .container {
    max-width: 500px;
    margin: 0 auto;
    background: #f1f5f9;
    padding: 20px;
  }
</style>
<div class="container">I'm centred on the page, with a maximum width of 500px.</div>

margin: 0 auto means "no top/bottom margin, and split the remaining space equally left and right". This is how almost every website centres its main content column.

Collapsing margins

When two vertical margins touch, they collapse into one: the bigger one wins instead of adding up.

<style>
  .a { margin-bottom: 40px; background: #fde68a; }
  .b { margin-top: 20px; background: #a7f3d0; }
</style>
<p class="a">Margin-bottom: 40px</p>
<p class="b">Margin-top: 20px. The gap between us is 40px, not 60px.</p>

This only happens with vertical margins between block elements, never with horizontal margins or padding, and not inside flex or grid containers. It surprises everyone at first; just remember the bigger margin wins.

A simple habit avoids most confusion: add spacing in one direction only, for example margin-bottom on elements, and margin-top: 0.

Negative margins

Margins can be negative, which pulls an element towards its neighbour or out of its container. Padding can't be negative. Use negative margins rarely; there's usually a clearer way.

Browser default spacing

Browsers add default margins to body, headings, paragraphs and lists. That's why there's a small gap around every unstyled page. Many projects start with a small reset:

body { margin: 0; }
h1, h2, h3, p { margin-top: 0; }

Common mistakes

  • Using padding when you need margin (or the reverse): if you want the background to grow, it's padding; if you want a gap between boxes, it's margin.
  • Getting the four-value order wrong. It's always clockwise from the top.
  • **margin: auto without a width**: a block already fills the full width, so there's nothing to centre.
  • Being surprised by collapsing margins.

Exercise

  1. Create three cards with padding: 20px and margin-bottom: 16px.
  2. Centre a 600px-wide container with margin: 0 auto.
  3. Make two buttons, one big and one small, using only padding and font size.
  4. Prove margin collapsing: give two paragraphs margins of 30px and 50px and measure the gap with developer tools (F12 → inspect).

Summary

  • Padding is space inside the border (shows the background); margin is space outside (transparent).
  • One to four values go clockwise: top, right, bottom, left.
  • margin: 0 auto centres a block that has a width.
  • Vertical margins between blocks collapse into the larger one.

Next, you'll put content, padding, border and margin together in the box model.
item.excerpt:encoded: The difference between padding (space inside) and margin (space outside), the one-to-four value shorthand, centring with auto, and collapsing margins.

item.title: CSS Box Model
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Every element on a web page is a rectangular box, even text and round avatars. The box model describes the layers of that box and how its final size is calculated. Once you understand it, layout bugs become much easier to fix.

The four layers

From the inside out:

  1. Content: the text, image or child elements.
  2. Padding: space around the content, inside the border.
  3. Border: the line around the padding.
  4. Margin: space outside the border, separating the box from others.
<style>
  .model {
    width: 200px;
    padding: 20px;
    border: 10px solid #2563eb;
    margin: 30px;
    background: #dbeafe;
  }
</style>
<div class="model">Content area</div>

How the width is calculated (the surprise)

By default, width sets the width of the content area only. Padding and border are added to it.

For the box above:

  200px  content
+  40px  padding (20 left + 20 right)
+  20px  border  (10 left + 10 right)
= 260px  visible width

Plus 30px of margin on each side, so it takes up 320px of space in total. Many beginners set width: 200px, add padding, and wonder why the box doesn't fit.

box-sizing: border-box

There's a better way. With box-sizing: border-box, the width includes the padding and border:

<style>
  .box {
    width: 200px;
    padding: 20px;
    border: 10px solid #334155;
    margin-bottom: 12px;
    background: #e2e8f0;
  }
  .content-box { box-sizing: content-box; }
  .border-box { box-sizing: border-box; }
</style>
<div class="box content-box">content-box: 260px wide</div>
<div class="box border-box">border-box: exactly 200px wide</div>

With border-box, the box is exactly as wide as you said, and the content shrinks to make room for padding and border. This is so much more intuitive that nearly every modern project starts with this rule:

*,
*::before,
*::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

Put it at the top of every stylesheet you write from now on.

A practical example: two columns that fit

<style>
  * { box-sizing: border-box; }
  .col {
    width: 50%;
    float: left;
    padding: 16px;
    border: 2px solid #94a3b8;
  }
</style>
<div class="col">Left column: 50% wide including padding and border.</div>
<div class="col">Right column: still fits next to the left one.</div>

Without border-box, each column would be 50% *plus* 36px, and the second one would drop below the first. (You'll learn better ways to make columns with Flexbox and Grid; this just shows the box model at work.)

Inline elements are different

Inline elements like <span>, <a> and <strong> follow the box model only partly:

  • width and height are ignored.
  • Left and right padding, border and margin push neighbours away.
  • Top and bottom padding and border are drawn, but don't push other lines away, so they can overlap.

To give an inline element a real size, change its display to inline-block or block. You'll learn about display in a later lesson.

Inspecting the box model

Every browser can show you the box model of any element:

  1. Right-click an element on any page → Inspect (or press F12).
  2. In the Styles or Computed panel, find the box diagram.
  3. It shows the exact content size, padding, border and margin. Hover over each layer to highlight it on the page.

This is the fastest way to find out why something is too wide or has an unexpected gap. Use it often.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that padding adds to width (without border-box), causing boxes to overflow.
  • Setting width on inline elements and wondering why nothing happens.
  • Using margin for space inside a coloured box. The background only fills content and padding.
  • Not using the developer tools to look at the box.

Exercise

  1. Create a box with width: 300px; padding: 25px; border: 5px solid; and calculate its visible width. Check your answer with developer tools.
  2. Add box-sizing: border-box and check again.
  3. Put the universal border-box rule at the top of your profile page project's CSS.
  4. Give a <span> a width of 200px, then change it to display: inline-block and compare.

Summary

  • Every element is a box: content, padding, border, margin.
  • By default, width is content only; padding and border are added.
  • box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border. Use it everywhere.
  • Inline elements ignore width and height; developer tools show every box's real size.

Next, you'll control element sizes with width, height, max-width and more.
item.excerpt:encoded: Every element is a box of content, padding, border and margin. Learn how its size is calculated, why box-sizing border-box makes life easier, and how to inspect boxes.

item.title: CSS Width and Height
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Sizing elements well is what separates layouts that break on phones from layouts that adapt to any screen. This lesson covers width and height, the units you can use, and the min and max properties that make sizes flexible.

Default sizes

  • Block elements (div, p, section) are as wide as their container and as tall as their content.
  • Inline elements are only as wide as their content, and ignore width and height.

Most of the time, the defaults are what you want. Set sizes only when you need to.

Setting width and height

<style>
  .box {
    width: 300px;
    height: 120px;
    background: #dbeafe;
    border: 2px solid #2563eb;
  }
</style>
<div class="box">300 × 120 pixels</div>

CSS units

rem is especially useful: if a user increases their browser's default font size, everything sized in rem grows with it, which is good for accessibility.

h1 { font-size: 2rem; }      /* 32px by default */
.card { padding: 1.5rem; }   /* 24px */

Percentages

<style>
  .parent { width: 400px; background: #f1f5f9; padding: 8px; }
  .child  { width: 50%; background: #93c5fd; }
</style>
<div class="parent">
  <div class="child">50% of 400px = 200px</div>
</div>

A percentage width is relative to the parent's content width.

max-width: the most useful size property

A fixed width breaks on small screens: a 900px box on a 375px phone causes horizontal scrolling. max-width fixes this:

<style>
  .article {
    max-width: 65ch;
    margin: 0 auto;
    padding: 0 16px;
    font-family: Georgia, serif;
    line-height: 1.7;
  }
</style>
<div class="article">
  <p>This column is never wider than about 65 characters, which is comfortable to read. On a narrow phone screen it simply shrinks to fit, with no horizontal scrolling. Resize the result pane to see it adapt.</p>
</div>

The box is as wide as possible up to the limit. This one property makes a layout work on everything from phones to wide monitors.

The same idea makes images responsive:

img {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

Images can shrink to fit their container but never grow beyond their real size, and height: auto keeps their proportions.

min-height instead of height

Fixed heights are risky: if the content grows (longer text, a translation, bigger font), it overflows the box. Prefer min-height, which lets the box grow:

<style>
  .fixed { height: 60px; background: #fecaca; margin-bottom: 30px; }
  .flexible { min-height: 60px; background: #bbf7d0; }
</style>
<div class="fixed">Fixed height: this long text doesn't fit in sixty pixels, so it spills out of the box and overlaps the next element when the box is narrow. That's the problem.</div>
<div class="flexible">min-height: at least 60px, but this box grows as tall as its content needs, so nothing ever spills out.</div>

A full-screen hero section is a classic use: min-height: 100vh;.

Overflow

When content is bigger than its box, overflow decides what happens:

.a { overflow: visible; } /* default: content spills out */
.b { overflow: hidden; }  /* extra content is cut off */
.c { overflow: auto; }    /* scrollbars appear only if needed */
<style>
  .scroll {
    height: 90px;
    overflow: auto;
    border: 1px solid #94a3b8;
    padding: 8px;
  }
</style>
<div class="scroll">
  <p>Line one</p><p>Line two</p><p>Line three</p><p>Line four</p><p>Line five</p>
</div>

overflow: auto is perfect for wide code blocks and tables on small screens. Use overflow-x or overflow-y to control just one direction.

aspect-ratio

.video-box {
  width: 100%;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
}

aspect-ratio keeps a box's proportions as its width changes. Great for video embeds and image placeholders.

Common mistakes

  • Fixed pixel widths on large elements, which cause horizontal scrolling on phones. Use max-width.
  • Fixed heights on text boxes, which overflow when content grows. Use min-height.
  • **height: 100% that does nothing**, because the parent has no defined height.
  • **Forgetting height: auto** when making images responsive, which squashes them.

Exercise

  1. Make a reading column with max-width: 65ch centred on the page.
  2. Make all images in your profile page responsive.
  3. Build a full-screen welcome section with min-height: 100vh.
  4. Put a long table inside a div with overflow-x: auto.

Summary

  • Blocks fill their container's width by default; inline elements ignore width and height.
  • Use rem for text and spacing, % and vw for fluid sizes, px for small fixed details.
  • max-width and min-height make layouts flexible; avoid fixed widths and heights.
  • overflow controls content that doesn't fit.

Next, you'll style text and fonts.
item.excerpt:encoded: Set sizes with px, %, rem, vw and vh, use max-width and min-height for flexible layouts, and control overflowing content.

item.title: CSS Text and Fonts
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Most of a website is text, so typography makes the biggest difference to how professional and readable it feels. In this lesson you'll choose fonts, size them, and control spacing, alignment and decoration.

font-family and fallbacks

body {
  font-family: "Inter", "Segoe UI", Roboto, Arial, sans-serif;
}

You list several fonts. The browser uses the first one available on the reader's device and falls back to the next. Always end with a generic family:

  • sans-serif: clean fonts without small strokes (Arial, Roboto). Good for screens.
  • serif: fonts with small strokes (Georgia, Times). Good for long articles.
  • monospace: every character the same width. For code.
  • system-ui: the operating system's own font. Fast and native-looking.

Put font names with spaces in quotes.

Web fonts

To use a font readers may not have installed, load it from a service like Google Fonts:

<head>
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
  <link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter:wght@400;600;700&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">
  <style>
    body { font-family: "Inter", sans-serif; }
  </style>
</head>

Every font file you load slows the page a little. Use one or two families and only the weights you need. display=swap shows text in a fallback font immediately, then swaps when the web font arrives.

Size, weight and style

<style>
  body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .big { font-size: 2rem; font-weight: 700; }
  .normal { font-size: 1rem; font-weight: 400; }
  .light { font-size: 0.875rem; font-weight: 300; color: #64748b; }
  .italic { font-style: italic; }
</style>
<p class="big">Bold, 2rem (32px)</p>
<p class="normal">Normal, 1rem (16px)</p>
<p class="light">Light, 0.875rem (14px)</p>
<p class="italic">Italic text</p>
  • font-size: use rem so text respects the reader's browser settings. 16px (1rem) is a good minimum for body text.
  • font-weight: 100–900; 400 is normal, 700 is bold. The font must include that weight.
  • font-style: normal or italic.

Line height: the readability secret

<style>
  .tight { line-height: 1.1; }
  .comfortable { line-height: 1.7; }
  p { max-width: 45ch; font-family: Georgia, serif; }
</style>
<p class="tight">Tight lines are hard to read because your eyes lose their place when jumping from the end of one line to the start of the next.</p>
<p class="comfortable">Comfortable spacing gives each line room to breathe, so long paragraphs feel easy instead of heavy.</p>

For body text, use a unitless line-height between 1.5 and 1.8. Headings can be tighter (1.1–1.3).

Text alignment

h1 { text-align: center; }
p  { text-align: left; }     /* default for English */
.price { text-align: right; }

justify stretches lines to fill the width, but it creates uneven gaps between words on the web. Keep long text left-aligned.

Decoration, transform and spacing

<style>
  a { text-decoration: none; color: #2563eb; }
  a:hover { text-decoration: underline; text-underline-offset: 3px; }
  .label { text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.08em; font-size: 0.75rem; font-weight: 600; }
  .old { text-decoration: line-through; color: #94a3b8; }
</style>
<p><a href="#">A link that underlines on hover</a></p>
<p class="label">Section label</p>
<p>Price: <span class="old">₹999</span> ₹499</p>
  • text-decoration: none, underline, line-through.
  • text-transform: uppercase, lowercase, capitalize. Keep the real text in normal case in the HTML; screen readers may spell out ALL-CAPS text letter by letter.
  • letter-spacing adds space between letters; small uppercase labels look better with a little extra.
  • word-spacing adds space between words.

Text shadow and overflow

.hero-title { text-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.4); }

.one-line {
  white-space: nowrap;
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;   /* shows "…" when text is cut */
}

A readable article style

<style>
  .post {
    font-family: Georgia, serif;
    font-size: 1.125rem;
    line-height: 1.75;
    color: #1f2937;
    max-width: 65ch;
    margin: 0 auto;
  }
  .post h2 {
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
    font-size: 1.5rem;
    line-height: 1.25;
    margin-top: 2em;
  }
</style>
<article class="post">
  <h2>Why typography matters</h2>
  <p>Good typography is invisible. Readers don't notice the font size, the line height or the width of the column; they just find the text easy and pleasant to read, and they stay longer.</p>
</article>

Common mistakes

  • Body text smaller than 16px.
  • No fallback fonts, or no generic family at the end.
  • Loading many font weights you never use.
  • Line height of 1 on paragraphs.
  • Very long lines of text across a wide screen. Limit to about 60–75 characters.

Exercise

  1. Load one Google Font and use it for headings, with a system font for body text.
  2. Set body text to 1.125rem with line height 1.7 and a max width of 65ch.
  3. Create a small uppercase "category label" with letter spacing.
  4. Make links lose their underline, and get it back on hover.

Summary

  • font-family takes a list with fallbacks, ending in a generic family.
  • Use rem for sizes, 400/700 weights, and line height around 1.6 for body text.
  • text-align, text-decoration, text-transform and letter-spacing fine-tune text.
  • Readable text = good size, generous line height, limited line length, strong contrast.

Next, you'll learn the display property, which controls how elements flow on the page.
item.excerpt:encoded: Font families and fallbacks, web fonts, size, weight and line height, alignment, decoration, transform and spacing, plus rules for readable text.

item.title: CSS Display
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
The display property decides how an element takes part in the layout: whether it starts on a new line, whether it accepts a width, whether it's shown at all, and whether its children are laid out with Flexbox or Grid. It's one of the most important properties in CSS.

block

div, p, h1, ul, section { display: block; } /* their default */

A block element:

  • Starts on a new line.
  • Fills the full width of its container (unless you set a width).
  • Accepts width, height, margin and padding on all sides.

inline

span, a, strong, em { display: inline; } /* their default */

An inline element:

  • Stays in the line of text.
  • Is only as wide as its content.
  • Ignores width and height; vertical margin has no effect.

inline-block: the best of both

<style>
  .tag {
    display: inline-block;
    padding: 4px 12px;
    margin: 4px;
    background: #e0e7ff;
    color: #3730a3;
    border-radius: 999px;
    font: 14px system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
</style>
<p>
  Topics:
  <a class="tag" href="#">HTML</a>
  <a class="tag" href="#">CSS</a>
  <a class="tag" href="#">JavaScript</a>
</p>

inline-block sits in the line like inline text, but accepts width, height and vertical padding like a block. It's perfect for tags, badges and buttons inside text.

Changing an element's display

Any element can be given any display. A classic example: turning a list into a horizontal menu:

<style>
  .menu { list-style: none; padding: 0; margin: 0; background: #1e293b; }
  .menu li { display: inline-block; }
  .menu a {
    display: block;
    padding: 12px 16px;
    color: white;
    text-decoration: none;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .menu a:hover { background: #334155; }
</style>
<ul class="menu">
  <li><a href="#">Home</a></li>
  <li><a href="#">Tutorials</a></li>
  <li><a href="#">Blog</a></li>
</ul>

The links are display: block so the whole padded area is clickable, not just the text. (In the Flexbox lessons you'll learn an even better way to build menus.)

Changing display only changes the look, never the meaning. A <span> with display: block is still a span.

display: none

.hidden { display: none; }

The element is removed from the page completely: it's not shown, takes up no space, and screen readers ignore it. JavaScript often toggles this to open and close menus, tabs and pop-ups.

Other ways to hide things

<style>
  .box { padding: 8px; margin: 4px 0; background: #dbeafe; }
  .invisible { visibility: hidden; }
  .faded { opacity: 0.3; }
</style>
<div class="box">Box 1</div>
<div class="box invisible">Box 2 (visibility: hidden)</div>
<div class="box">Box 3</div>
<div class="box faded">Box 4 (opacity: 0.3)</div>

Hiding visually but keeping it for screen readers

Sometimes text should be read aloud but not shown, like a label for an icon button. Use this well-known class:

.visually-hidden {
  position: absolute;
  width: 1px;
  height: 1px;
  padding: 0;
  margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip: rect(0, 0, 0, 0);
  white-space: nowrap;
  border: 0;
}

flex and grid

Two more values turn an element into a layout container for its children:

.row { display: flex; }   /* children line up in a row */
.grid { display: grid; }  /* children placed on a grid */
<style>
  .row { display: flex; gap: 8px; }
  .row div { background: #fde68a; padding: 12px; }
</style>
<div class="row">
  <div>One</div>
  <div>Two</div>
  <div>Three</div>
</div>

These are how modern layouts are built, and they get four lessons of their own, starting soon.

Common mistakes

  • Setting width on an inline element and seeing no change. Use inline-block or block.
  • Small clickable areas because links stay inline inside menus. Make them block and add padding.
  • **Using opacity: 0 to hide content**, which screen readers still read and which can still be clicked.
  • Changing display to change meaning. Pick the right HTML element first.

Exercise

  1. Make a row of three "badge" links with inline-block, padding and rounded corners.
  2. Turn a vertical list into a horizontal menu.
  3. Hide one box with display: none and another with visibility: hidden; compare the gaps.
  4. Add a visually hidden text label to an icon-only button.

Summary

  • block starts a new line and fills the width; inline flows with text and ignores sizes.
  • inline-block flows with text but accepts sizes.
  • display: none removes an element; visibility: hidden hides it but keeps its space.
  • flex and grid make an element a layout container for its children.

Next, you'll position elements precisely with the position property.
item.excerpt:encoded: How the display property controls layout: block, inline, inline-block, none, flex and grid, plus hiding elements correctly with display none and visibility.

item.title: CSS Position
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Normally, elements are placed one after another in the "normal flow" of the page. The position property lets you move an element out of that flow: pin a badge to the corner of a card, keep a header at the top while scrolling, or float a button over the page.

The five values

The offset properties top, right, bottom and left say where to place the element.

relative

<style>
  .nudge { position: relative; top: 10px; left: 20px; background: #fde68a; }
</style>
<p>Normal paragraph.</p>
<p class="nudge">I'm moved 10px down and 20px right from where I'd normally be.</p>
<p>The space I left behind is kept, so nothing else moves.</p>

You'll rarely nudge things like this. The main use of relative is as a container for absolutely positioned children.

absolute

An absolute element is placed relative to its nearest ancestor that has a position other than static. If there's none, it's placed relative to the page.

<style>
  .card {
    position: relative;   /* the reference box */
    width: 260px;
    padding: 20px;
    border: 1px solid #e2e8f0;
    border-radius: 12px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .badge {
    position: absolute;
    top: -10px;
    right: -10px;
    background: #ef4444;
    color: white;
    font-size: 12px;
    font-weight: 700;
    padding: 4px 10px;
    border-radius: 999px;
  }
</style>
<div class="card">
  <span class="badge">NEW</span>
  <h3>JavaScript course</h3>
  <p>25 lessons with live examples.</p>
</div>

The pattern to remember: **parent relative, child absolute.** The badge is pinned to the top-right corner of the card wherever the card goes.

Absolute elements are taken out of the flow: other elements act as if they don't exist, so they can overlap content.

Overlay text on an image

<style>
  .photo { position: relative; width: 300px; }
  .photo img { display: block; width: 100%; height: auto; border-radius: 8px; }
  .photo figcaption {
    position: absolute;
    left: 0; right: 0; bottom: 0;
    padding: 10px;
    background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.6);
    color: white;
    border-radius: 0 0 8px 8px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
</style>
<figure class="photo">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1011/600/400" alt="A woman in a canoe on a lake" width="600" height="400">
  <figcaption>Morning on the lake</figcaption>
</figure>

Setting both left: 0 and right: 0 stretches the caption across the full width.

fixed

.back-to-top {
  position: fixed;
  right: 20px;
  bottom: 20px;
}

A fixed element stays in the same spot in the window while the page scrolls: chat buttons, cookie notices, "back to top" buttons. Keep fixed elements small, especially on phones, so they don't cover the content.

sticky

<style>
  .sticky-head {
    position: sticky;
    top: 0;
    background: #1e293b;
    color: white;
    padding: 10px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .filler { height: 600px; background: linear-gradient(#f8fafc, #cbd5e1); padding: 10px; }
</style>
<div class="sticky-head">I stick to the top when you scroll the result pane</div>
<div class="filler">Scroll down…</div>

A sticky element behaves normally until it reaches the top value while scrolling, then sticks there until its parent scrolls out of view. It's ideal for table headers, section headings and sidebars. It needs a top (or bottom) value to work, and it stops working if an ancestor has overflow: hidden.

z-index: what's on top

When positioned elements overlap, z-index decides which is in front. Higher numbers are closer to the viewer:

.dropdown { position: absolute; z-index: 10; }
.modal    { position: fixed;    z-index: 100; }

z-index only works on positioned elements (and flex/grid children). Keep a simple scale like 1, 10, 100 instead of random huge numbers like 99999.

Common mistakes

  • Absolute child with no positioned parent, so it flies to the corner of the whole page. Add position: relative to the parent.
  • Using absolute positioning for page layout. Use Flexbox and Grid; absolute is for small decorations and overlays.
  • Sticky that doesn't stick, because there's no top value or a parent has overflow: hidden.
  • Fixed elements covering content on small screens.

Exercise

  1. Add a "SALE" badge to the corner of a product card.
  2. Put a caption over the bottom of an image.
  3. Create a fixed "↑ Top" button in the bottom-right corner that links to #top.
  4. Make a long table whose header row sticks while scrolling (th { position: sticky; top: 0; }).

Summary

  • relative keeps the element in flow and creates a reference box.
  • absolute places an element inside its nearest positioned ancestor.
  • fixed pins to the window; sticky sticks after scrolling to a point.
  • z-index controls stacking order of positioned elements.

Next, you'll start modern layout with Flexbox.
item.excerpt:encoded: Static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky positioning explained with badges, overlays, sticky headers and back-to-top buttons, plus z-index stacking.

item.title: CSS Flexbox Basics
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Flexbox is a layout system for arranging items in one direction, a row or a column, and distributing space between them. It solved problems that used to need hacks, like vertical centring and equal-height columns, and it's now the everyday tool for menus, toolbars, cards and forms.

The flex container

Flexbox works on a parent and its direct children. Add display: flex to the parent:

<style>
  .container {
    display: flex;
    background: #f1f5f9;
    padding: 10px;
  }
  .item {
    background: #3b82f6;
    color: white;
    padding: 16px;
    margin: 4px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
</style>
<div class="container">
  <div class="item">1</div>
  <div class="item">2</div>
  <div class="item">3</div>
</div>

The parent is the flex container; its children are flex items. The items now sit side by side in a row.

The two axes

Flexbox thinks in two directions:

  • The main axis: the direction items are placed in (horizontal by default).
  • The cross axis: at right angles to it (vertical by default).

justify-content arranges items along the main axis; align-items along the cross axis. Keep this in mind and the rest of Flexbox makes sense.

flex-direction

.container { flex-direction: row; }            /* default: left to right */
.container { flex-direction: column; }         /* top to bottom */
.container { flex-direction: row-reverse; }
.container { flex-direction: column-reverse; }

With column, the main axis becomes vertical, so justify-content and align-items swap their visual direction.

justify-content: spacing on the main axis

<style>
  .row { display: flex; background: #f1f5f9; margin-bottom: 8px; font: 13px system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .row span { background: #8b5cf6; color: white; padding: 8px 14px; margin: 3px; }
</style>
<div class="row" style="justify-content: flex-start;"><span>start</span><span>B</span><span>C</span></div>
<div class="row" style="justify-content: center;"><span>center</span><span>B</span><span>C</span></div>
<div class="row" style="justify-content: flex-end;"><span>end</span><span>B</span><span>C</span></div>
<div class="row" style="justify-content: space-between;"><span>between</span><span>B</span><span>C</span></div>
<div class="row" style="justify-content: space-around;"><span>around</span><span>B</span><span>C</span></div>
<div class="row" style="justify-content: space-evenly;"><span>evenly</span><span>B</span><span>C</span></div>

space-between is the classic choice for a header with a logo on the left and a menu on the right.

align-items: alignment on the cross axis

<style>
  .tall { display: flex; height: 120px; background: #f1f5f9; margin-bottom: 8px; font: 13px system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .tall span { background: #10b981; color: white; padding: 8px 14px; margin: 3px; }
</style>
<div class="tall" style="align-items: stretch;"><span>stretch (default)</span><span>B</span></div>
<div class="tall" style="align-items: flex-start;"><span>flex-start</span><span>B</span></div>
<div class="tall" style="align-items: center;"><span>center</span><span>B</span></div>
<div class="tall" style="align-items: flex-end;"><span>flex-end</span><span>B</span></div>

The default, stretch, makes all items the same height, which is why flex columns are equal height for free.

Perfect centring

The famous "how do I centre a div?" question, answered in three lines:

<style>
  .center {
    display: flex;
    justify-content: center;
    align-items: center;
    height: 200px;
    background: #0f172a;
  }
  .center p { color: white; font: 20px system-ui, sans-serif; }
</style>
<div class="center"><p>Perfectly centred</p></div>

gap

.container {
  display: flex;
  gap: 16px;        /* space between items */
  /* row-gap and column-gap can be set separately */
}

gap puts space between items only, not on the outer edges. It's much cleaner than adding margins to every item.

flex-wrap

By default, flex items stay on one line and shrink to fit. With flex-wrap: wrap, they move to a new line when there's no room:

<style>
  .tags { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px; max-width: 300px; }
  .tags span { background: #e0e7ff; padding: 6px 12px; border-radius: 999px; font: 14px system-ui, sans-serif; }
</style>
<div class="tags">
  <span>HTML</span><span>CSS</span><span>JavaScript</span><span>Python</span>
  <span>SQL</span><span>Git</span><span>React</span><span>Node.js</span>
</div>

Use align-content to control the spacing between wrapped lines.

A real example: a site header

<style>
  .header {
    display: flex;
    justify-content: space-between;
    align-items: center;
    gap: 16px;
    padding: 12px 20px;
    background: #1e293b;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .logo { color: white; font-weight: 700; font-size: 20px; }
  .nav { display: flex; gap: 16px; }
  .nav a { color: #cbd5e1; text-decoration: none; }
  .nav a:hover { color: white; }
</style>
<header class="header">
  <div class="logo">VitalStack</div>
  <nav class="nav">
    <a href="#">Tutorials</a>
    <a href="#">Blog</a>
    <a href="#">Contact</a>
  </nav>
</header>

Two flex containers: the header (logo vs nav) and the nav itself (the links).

Common mistakes

  • **Putting display: flex on the items** instead of their parent.
  • Mixing up the axes after changing flex-direction to column.
  • Using margins for spacing between items when gap does it better.
  • **Forgetting flex-wrap**, so items squash instead of moving to a new line on phones.

Exercise

  1. Build the header example, then add a "Sign in" button on the far right.
  2. Centre a card in the middle of a 300px-tall box.
  3. Make a wrapping list of tag "pills" with gap.
  4. Change a row to flex-direction: column and see how justify-content now works vertically.

Summary

  • display: flex on a parent lays out its direct children in a row (or column).
  • justify-content spaces items on the main axis; align-items aligns them on the cross axis.
  • gap adds space between items; flex-wrap: wrap lets them flow onto new lines.
  • Flexbox makes centring and equal-height items easy.

Next, you'll control how flex items grow and shrink to build real layouts.
item.excerpt:encoded: Lay out items in a row or column with Flexbox: flex containers, direction, justify-content, align-items, gap and wrapping, with a visual example of each.

item.title: CSS Flexbox Layouts
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
In the last lesson you arranged items with properties on the container. Now you'll control the items themselves: how much they grow, shrink and how wide they start. With these, you can build most everyday layouts.

flex-grow: sharing extra space

<style>
  .row { display: flex; gap: 6px; background: #f1f5f9; padding: 6px; margin-bottom: 8px; font: 14px system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .row div { background: #3b82f6; color: white; padding: 12px; }
</style>
<div class="row">
  <div>No grow</div>
  <div style="flex-grow: 1;">flex-grow: 1 (takes all the extra space)</div>
</div>
<div class="row">
  <div style="flex-grow: 1;">grow 1</div>
  <div style="flex-grow: 2;">grow 2 (gets twice as much extra space)</div>
</div>

flex-grow decides how the leftover space in the container is shared. 0 (the default) means "don't grow". If one item has 1 and the rest have 0, that item takes all the extra room. This is how you make a search box fill the space next to a button.

flex-shrink: giving up space

When there isn't enough room, items shrink. flex-shrink: 1 is the default (shrink if needed); flex-shrink: 0 means "never shrink below my size". Use it for things like icons and avatars that must keep their size.

flex-basis: the starting size

flex-basis sets an item's size before extra space is shared out. It works like width in a row (or height in a column):

.sidebar { flex-basis: 250px; }

The flex shorthand

You'll usually write all three together with flex: grow shrink basis:

.item { flex: 1; }           /* = 1 1 0%: share space equally */
.item { flex: 0 0 250px; }   /* fixed 250px: don't grow, don't shrink */
.item { flex: 1 1 200px; }   /* start at 200px, grow and shrink as needed */

flex: 1 on every item gives equal-width columns, whatever their content.

Layout 1: sidebar + main content

<style>
  .layout { display: flex; gap: 16px; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .sidebar { flex: 0 0 200px; background: #e2e8f0; padding: 16px; }
  .main { flex: 1; background: #f8fafc; padding: 16px; border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; }
</style>
<div class="layout">
  <aside class="sidebar">Sidebar: always 200px</aside>
  <main class="main">Main content: takes all the remaining width. Resize the result pane and watch it adapt while the sidebar keeps its size.</main>
</div>

Layout 2: equal cards with buttons at the bottom

<style>
  .cards { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 16px; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .card {
    flex: 1 1 200px;
    display: flex;
    flex-direction: column;
    border: 1px solid #e2e8f0;
    border-radius: 10px;
    padding: 16px;
  }
  .card p { flex: 1; color: #475569; }
  .card a { background: #2563eb; color: white; padding: 8px; text-align: center; border-radius: 6px; text-decoration: none; }
</style>
<div class="cards">
  <div class="card"><h3>HTML</h3><p>Short text.</p><a href="#">Start</a></div>
  <div class="card"><h3>CSS</h3><p>This card has a much longer description, but its button still lines up with the others at the bottom.</p><a href="#">Start</a></div>
  <div class="card"><h3>JavaScript</h3><p>Medium-length text here.</p><a href="#">Start</a></div>
</div>

Two tricks at once:

  • flex: 1 1 200px with flex-wrap: wrap makes cards share the row equally but drop to a new line when they'd be narrower than 200px: a responsive grid with no media queries.
  • Each card is itself a column flex container, and the paragraph has flex: 1, so it stretches and pushes every button to the bottom.

Layout 3: input with a button

<style>
  .search { display: flex; max-width: 420px; }
  .search input { flex: 1; padding: 10px; border: 1px solid #94a3b8; border-right: 0; border-radius: 8px 0 0 8px; min-width: 0; }
  .search button { flex: 0 0 auto; padding: 10px 16px; border: 0; background: #2563eb; color: white; border-radius: 0 8px 8px 0; }
</style>
<form class="search">
  <input type="search" aria-label="Search lessons" placeholder="Search lessons">
  <button>Search</button>
</form>

The input grows; the button keeps its natural size. min-width: 0 lets the input shrink below its default width on tiny screens.

Layout 4: footer at the bottom of short pages

body {
  min-height: 100vh;
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  margin: 0;
}
main { flex: 1; }

The <main> grows to fill any empty space, so the footer always sits at the bottom of the window, even on a page with little content.

Pushing one item away with margin auto

.nav { display: flex; gap: 12px; }
.nav .signin { margin-left: auto; }

An auto margin in a flex container eats all the free space on that side, pushing the item to the far end. Great for a "Sign in" link at the end of a menu.

order and align-self

  • order: -1 moves an item earlier visually (without changing the HTML). Use with care: keyboard and screen reader order still follow the HTML.
  • align-self: center overrides align-items for one item.

Common mistakes

  • **Expecting flex: 1 to work without display: flex** on the parent.
  • Content overflowing because of long words or inputs: add min-width: 0 to the flex item.
  • **Using order to fix the HTML order**, which confuses keyboard users. Fix the HTML instead.

Exercise

  1. Build a page with a 240px sidebar and fluid main area.
  2. Make three cards with different text lengths and buttons aligned at the bottom.
  3. Add a "Sign in" link pushed to the right end of a nav with margin-left: auto.
  4. Make a footer stick to the bottom of a short page.

Summary

  • flex-grow shares extra space, flex-shrink handles too little space, flex-basis sets the starting size.
  • flex: 1 = equal shares; flex: 0 0 250px = fixed size.
  • Nested flex containers solve layouts like equal cards with bottom-aligned buttons.
  • margin-left: auto pushes an item to the end.

Next, you'll learn CSS Grid, the two-dimensional layout system.
item.excerpt:encoded: Control flex items with flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis and the flex shorthand, then build a sidebar layout, equal cards, a sticky footer and a media object.

item.title: CSS Grid Basics
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Flexbox arranges items in one direction. CSS Grid arranges them in two directions at once: rows and columns. It's the best tool for page layouts, galleries and any design that lines up both horizontally and vertically.

A first grid

<style>
  .grid {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 150px 150px 150px;
    gap: 10px;
  }
  .grid div {
    background: #3b82f6;
    color: white;
    padding: 20px;
    text-align: center;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
</style>
<div class="grid">
  <div>1</div><div>2</div><div>3</div>
  <div>4</div><div>5</div><div>6</div>
</div>
  • display: grid makes the parent a grid container; its direct children become grid items.
  • grid-template-columns defines the columns: here, three columns of 150px.
  • Items fill the cells in order, left to right, then wrap onto the next row automatically.

The fr unit

Fixed pixel columns don't adapt to the screen. The fr unit (fraction) shares the available space:

<style>
  .g { display: grid; gap: 8px; margin-bottom: 10px; font: 14px system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .g div { background: #10b981; color: white; padding: 12px; }
</style>
<div class="g" style="grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;">
  <div>1fr</div><div>1fr</div><div>1fr</div>
</div>
<div class="g" style="grid-template-columns: 2fr 1fr;">
  <div>2fr (twice as wide)</div><div>1fr</div>
</div>
<div class="g" style="grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;">
  <div>200px</div><div>1fr (the rest)</div>
</div>

You can mix units: 200px 1fr is a classic sidebar layout.

repeat()

Instead of writing 1fr many times:

grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);         /* 4 equal columns */
grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) 200px;   /* 3 equal + one fixed */

Rows

Rows are created automatically as items need them, each as tall as its content. You can set them explicitly too:

.grid {
  grid-template-rows: 80px 1fr 60px;
  grid-auto-rows: 150px; /* height of any extra, automatically created rows */
}

gap

.grid {
  gap: 16px;            /* between rows and columns */
  row-gap: 24px;        /* or set them separately */
  column-gap: 12px;
}

Placing items across cells

Grid lines are numbered starting at 1 on the left (and top). An item can start and end at any line:

<style>
  .board {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
    grid-auto-rows: 80px;
    gap: 8px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .board div { background: #e0e7ff; padding: 8px; border-radius: 6px; }
  .wide { grid-column: span 2; background: #c7d2fe !important; }
  .tall { grid-row: span 2; background: #a5b4fc !important; }
  .full { grid-column: 1 / -1; background: #818cf8 !important; color: white; }
</style>
<div class="board">
  <div class="full">Full width (1 / -1)</div>
  <div class="wide">Spans 2 columns</div>
  <div class="tall">Spans 2 rows</div>
  <div>4</div>
  <div>5</div>
  <div>6</div>
  <div>7</div>
</div>
  • grid-column: span 2 makes an item two columns wide.
  • grid-row: span 2 makes it two rows tall.
  • grid-column: 1 / -1 stretches from the first line to the last: full width. Negative numbers count from the end.
  • You can also write exact lines: grid-column: 2 / 4 covers columns 2 and 3.

Aligning items in their cells

.grid {
  justify-items: center;  /* horizontal alignment inside cells */
  align-items: center;    /* vertical alignment inside cells */
  place-items: center;    /* both at once */
}

The shortest way to centre anything: display: grid; place-items: center;.

A photo gallery

<style>
  .gallery {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
    gap: 6px;
  }
  .gallery img { width: 100%; height: 120px; object-fit: cover; display: block; border-radius: 6px; }
  .gallery img:first-child { grid-column: span 2; grid-row: span 2; height: 100%; }
</style>
<div class="gallery">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/10/400/300" alt="Forest" width="400" height="300">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/11/300/200" alt="Hills" width="300" height="200">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/12/300/200" alt="Beach" width="300" height="200">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/13/300/200" alt="Coast" width="300" height="200">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/14/300/200" alt="Sea" width="300" height="200">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/15/300/200" alt="Waterfall" width="300" height="200">
</div>

Grid or Flexbox?

They work together: a grid page layout often contains flex components.

Common mistakes

  • Grid on the wrong element. display: grid goes on the parent.
  • Forgetting that only direct children become grid items.
  • Fixed pixel columns that overflow on phones. Use fr and the responsive tricks in the next lesson.
  • Off-by-one line numbers. Three columns have four lines (1 to 4).

Exercise

  1. Make a 4-column grid of 8 boxes with a 12px gap.
  2. Make the first box span the full width as a header.
  3. Build a 250px 1fr layout with a sidebar and content.
  4. Build the photo gallery with your own images and make the first photo big.

Summary

  • display: grid + grid-template-columns creates a grid.
  • fr shares free space; repeat() saves typing; gap spaces cells.
  • grid-column and grid-row with span or line numbers place items across cells.
  • Use Grid for two-dimensional layouts and Flexbox for one-dimensional ones.

Next, you'll build complete page layouts with named grid areas and responsive grids.
item.excerpt:encoded: Build two-dimensional layouts with CSS Grid: grid containers, columns and rows, the fr unit, repeat(), gap, and placing items across several cells.

item.title: CSS Grid Layouts
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
With the basics of Grid in place, you can build complete page layouts. Two features make Grid especially powerful: named areas, which let you draw your layout in the CSS, and auto-fit with minmax(), which makes grids responsive without a single media query.

Named grid areas

grid-template-areas lets you name regions of the grid and arrange them like a map:

<style>
  .page {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
    grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
    grid-template-areas:
      "header  header"
      "sidebar main"
      "footer  footer";
    gap: 10px;
    min-height: 360px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .page > * { padding: 16px; border-radius: 8px; }
  .page header { grid-area: header; background: #1e293b; color: white; }
  .page aside  { grid-area: sidebar; background: #e2e8f0; }
  .page main   { grid-area: main; background: #f8fafc; border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; }
  .page footer { grid-area: footer; background: #cbd5e1; }
</style>
<div class="page">
  <header>Header</header>
  <aside>Sidebar</aside>
  <main>Main content</main>
  <footer>Footer</footer>
</div>
  • Each string in grid-template-areas is one row; each word is one cell.
  • Repeating a name (header header) makes that area span those cells.
  • Each item is assigned with grid-area: name.
  • A . means an empty cell.

The CSS now looks like a picture of the layout, which makes it easy to read and change.

Rearranging for phones

The real magic: to change the layout on small screens, you only redraw the map. You'll learn media queries properly in the next lesson; here's a preview:

@media (max-width: 600px) {
  .page {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
    grid-template-areas:
      "header"
      "main"
      "sidebar"
      "footer";
  }
}

On phones, everything stacks in one column, and the sidebar moves below the main content. The HTML doesn't change.

Responsive cards with auto-fit and minmax()

This one line creates a card grid that adapts to any screen width:

<style>
  .cards {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr));
    gap: 14px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .cards article {
    border: 1px solid #e2e8f0;
    border-radius: 10px;
    padding: 16px;
    background: white;
  }
</style>
<div class="cards">
  <article><h3>HTML</h3><p>Structure</p></article>
  <article><h3>CSS</h3><p>Style</p></article>
  <article><h3>JavaScript</h3><p>Behaviour</p></article>
  <article><h3>SQL</h3><p>Data</p></article>
  <article><h3>Python</h3><p>Everything else</p></article>
</div>

Resize the result pane and the number of columns changes by itself. Here's how it works:

  • minmax(180px, 1fr): each column is at least 180px, and at most one equal share of the space.
  • repeat(auto-fit, …): create as many columns as fit.

On a phone you get one column; on a laptop, four or five. No media queries needed.

auto-fit vs auto-fill

  • auto-fit stretches the existing items to fill the row when there are only a few.
  • auto-fill keeps empty "ghost" columns, so a few items stay at their minimum width.

For card grids, auto-fit is usually what you want.

A blog layout

<style>
  .blog {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) 260px;
    gap: 24px;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .posts {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr));
    gap: 16px;
  }
  .post { border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; border-radius: 10px; overflow: hidden; }
  .post img { width: 100%; height: 110px; object-fit: cover; display: block; }
  .post h3 { font-size: 16px; margin: 10px 12px 14px; }
  .side { background: #f1f5f9; padding: 16px; border-radius: 10px; align-self: start; }
</style>
<div class="blog">
  <div class="posts">
    <article class="post"><img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1/400/220" alt="" width="400" height="220"><h3>Getting started with Git</h3></article>
    <article class="post"><img src="https://picsum.photos/id/2/400/220" alt="" width="400" height="220"><h3>10 VS Code shortcuts</h3></article>
    <article class="post"><img src="https://picsum.photos/id/3/400/220" alt="" width="400" height="220"><h3>What is an API?</h3></article>
  </div>
  <aside class="side"><h3>Popular</h3><p>CSS Flexbox Basics</p><p>Python Lists</p></aside>
</div>

The outer grid makes two columns: posts and sidebar. The inner grid is a responsive card grid. minmax(0, 1fr) stops long content from stretching the column. align-self: start keeps the sidebar from stretching to the full height.

Grid and Flexbox together

A good rule of thumb:

  • Grid for the overall layout (the page, the card grid).
  • Flexbox inside components (the content of each card, a header's nav links, a button with an icon).

You don't have to choose one. Most modern sites use both, often on the same page.

Common mistakes

  • Area names that don't form rectangles. Each named area must be a rectangle; L-shapes aren't allowed.
  • Different numbers of cells in each row of grid-template-areas.
  • **Forgetting grid-area** on the items, so they ignore the map.
  • Columns that overflow because of long words or wide images: use minmax(0, 1fr) and max-width: 100% on images.

Exercise

  1. Build the header / sidebar / main / footer layout with named areas.
  2. Add the media query so it stacks on narrow screens, with the sidebar under the main content.
  3. Create a responsive grid of 8 cards with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)).
  4. Inside each card, use Flexbox to put an icon and a title side by side.

Summary

  • grid-template-areas draws the layout; grid-area places items.
  • Redraw the areas in a media query to rearrange the layout for phones.
  • repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min, 1fr)) creates responsive grids without media queries.
  • Use Grid for layout and Flexbox for components.

Next, you'll make every page work on phones, tablets and desktops with responsive design and media queries.

item.title: CSS Responsive Design and Media Queries
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Most people visit websites on their phones. Responsive design means one page that adapts its layout to any screen, from a small phone to a wide monitor. In this lesson you'll learn the tools: the viewport tag, flexible sizes, media queries and fluid typography.

Step 1: the viewport meta tag

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

Without this line in the <head>, phones pretend to be a 980px-wide desktop and shrink the whole page down to tiny, unreadable text. With it, the page uses the phone's real width. Every responsive page needs it.

Step 2: flexible foundations

Much of responsive design is just avoiding fixed sizes. You've already learned the basics:

  • max-width instead of width for containers.
  • max-width: 100%; height: auto; for images.
  • fr, % and flex for columns.
  • rem for text and spacing.
  • repeat(auto-fit, minmax(...)) for card grids.

Get these right and a page is already 80% responsive before you write a single media query.

Media queries

A media query applies CSS only when a condition is true, usually a minimum or maximum screen width:

<style>
  .banner {
    padding: 16px;
    background: #fde68a;
    font: 18px system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  @media (min-width: 600px) {
    .banner { background: #a7f3d0; }
    .banner::after { content: " (600px or wider)"; }
  }
  @media (min-width: 900px) {
    .banner { background: #bfdbfe; }
    .banner::after { content: " (900px or wider)"; }
  }
</style>
<div class="banner">Resize the result pane</div>

The rules inside @media (min-width: 600px) { … } only apply when the window is at least 600px wide.

Mobile-first

There are two ways to write media queries:

  • Desktop-first: write the desktop layout, then use max-width queries to fix it for smaller screens.
  • Mobile-first: write the simple phone layout first (with no media query), then use min-width queries to add columns as space grows.

Mobile-first is the recommended approach: phone layouts are usually simpler (one column), so you start simple and add complexity, instead of undoing it.

<style>
  .layout { display: grid; gap: 12px; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .layout > div { background: #e0e7ff; padding: 16px; border-radius: 8px; }

  /* Tablets: two columns */
  @media (min-width: 600px) {
    .layout { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }
  }

  /* Desktops: sidebar + main + sidebar */
  @media (min-width: 900px) {
    .layout { grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 200px; }
  }
</style>
<div class="layout">
  <div>Menu</div>
  <div>Main content</div>
  <div>Related links</div>
</div>

Choosing breakpoints

A breakpoint is a width where the layout changes. Don't design for particular phone models; there are thousands. Instead, widen the browser slowly and add a breakpoint where the design starts to look wrong. Common starting points:

Two or three breakpoints are enough for most sites.

A responsive navigation

<style>
  .nav { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; background: #1e293b; padding: 12px; }
  .nav ul { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 0; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 4px; }
  .nav a { color: white; text-decoration: none; display: block; padding: 8px; }

  @media (min-width: 600px) {
    .nav ul { flex-direction: row; gap: 16px; }
  }
</style>
<nav class="nav">
  <ul>
    <li><a href="#">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="#">Tutorials</a></li>
    <li><a href="#">Blog</a></li>
    <li><a href="#">Contact</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

Stacked on phones, in a row on larger screens. (A real site often hides the menu behind a "☰" button on phones; that needs a little JavaScript, which you'll learn in the JavaScript course.)

Fluid typography with clamp()

Headings that look great on a desktop are often too big on a phone. clamp() scales text smoothly between a minimum and maximum:

h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 4vw + 1rem, 3rem);
}

clamp(min, preferred, max): the heading is never smaller than 1.75rem, never larger than 3rem, and scales with the window width in between. No breakpoints needed.

Other useful media features

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  body { background: #0f172a; color: #e2e8f0; }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * { animation: none !important; transition: none !important; }
}

@media (hover: hover) {
  .card:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); }
}

@media print {
  nav, footer, .ads { display: none; }
}
  • prefers-color-scheme: the user's light or dark mode setting.
  • prefers-reduced-motion: the user asked for less animation (some people get dizzy).
  • hover: whether the device can hover (phones can't).
  • print: styles for printing.

Testing responsive pages

  • Browser device mode: press F12, then the phone/tablet icon (Ctrl + Shift + M). Choose sizes or drag the width.
  • Test on a real phone, too: touch targets, font sizes and fixed elements feel different in your hand.
  • Check that there's no horizontal scrolling at 320px wide, the narrowest common phone width.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the viewport meta tag.
  • Fixed widths like width: 960px on containers.
  • Too many breakpoints for specific devices.
  • Tiny tap targets. Buttons and links should be at least about 44 × 44 pixels on touch screens.
  • Hiding important content on mobile. Phone users need the same information.

Exercise

  1. Take your profile page and make it mobile-first: one column by default.
  2. At 700px, show the skills and projects sections side by side.
  3. Make the main heading fluid with clamp().
  4. Add a prefers-color-scheme: dark block with dark colours.
  5. Test it at 320px, 768px and 1280px widths in device mode.

Summary

  • Always include the viewport meta tag.
  • Flexible units and layouts do most of the work; media queries handle the rest.
  • Write mobile-first CSS and add min-width breakpoints where the design needs them.
  • clamp() makes text fluid; media features handle dark mode, motion, hover and print.

Next, you'll add smooth movement with CSS transitions.

item.title: CSS Transitions and Transforms
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
When a button changes colour on hover, the change normally happens instantly. A transition makes it happen smoothly over a short time. Combined with transforms (move, scale, rotate), transitions give a site a polished, responsive feel with very little code.

A first transition

<style>
  .btn {
    background: #2563eb;
    color: white;
    border: none;
    padding: 12px 24px;
    border-radius: 8px;
    font-size: 16px;
    transition: background-color 0.3s ease;
  }
  .btn:hover {
    background-color: #1e3a8a;
  }
</style>
<button class="btn">Hover over me</button>

The transition goes on the normal state, not the hover state, so the change animates both when the mouse arrives and when it leaves.

The parts of a transition

transition: property duration timing-function delay;
  • property: what to animate (background-color, transform, opacity), or all.
  • duration: how long, e.g. 0.2s or 200ms.
  • timing function: the speed curve.
  • delay (optional): wait before starting.

Several properties can be listed with commas:

.card {
  transition: transform 0.2s ease, box-shadow 0.2s ease;
}

Avoid transition: all: it can animate things you didn't intend and is slower.

Timing functions

<style>
  .track { background: #f1f5f9; margin-bottom: 6px; padding: 4px; font: 13px system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .ball {
    width: 90px; padding: 6px; background: #8b5cf6; color: white; border-radius: 999px; text-align: center;
    transition: transform 1.2s;
  }
  .tracks:hover .ball { transform: translateX(220px); }
</style>
<div class="tracks">
  <p>Hover over this area:</p>
  <div class="track"><div class="ball" style="transition-timing-function: linear;">linear</div></div>
  <div class="track"><div class="ball" style="transition-timing-function: ease;">ease</div></div>
  <div class="track"><div class="ball" style="transition-timing-function: ease-in;">ease-in</div></div>
  <div class="track"><div class="ball" style="transition-timing-function: ease-out;">ease-out</div></div>
  <div class="track"><div class="ball" style="transition-timing-function: ease-in-out;">ease-in-out</div></div>
</div>
  • ease (default): starts fast, ends slow. Good general choice.
  • ease-out: fast start, gentle stop. Great for things appearing.
  • ease-in: slow start. Good for things leaving.
  • linear: constant speed. Mostly for spinners.
  • cubic-bezier(...) creates custom curves.

Transforms

transform changes how an element is drawn without affecting the layout around it:

transform: translateX(20px);       /* move right */
transform: translateY(-4px);       /* move up */
transform: scale(1.05);            /* 5% bigger */
transform: rotate(45deg);          /* rotate */
transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.02);  /* combine several */

Because transforms don't move other elements, they're smooth and cheap for the browser to animate.

A lifting card

<style>
  body { background: #f1f5f9; padding: 30px; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .card {
    width: 240px;
    background: white;
    padding: 20px;
    border-radius: 12px;
    box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1);
    transition: transform 0.2s ease, box-shadow 0.2s ease;
  }
  .card:hover {
    transform: translateY(-6px);
    box-shadow: 0 12px 24px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15);
  }
</style>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Hover me</h3>
  <p>I lift up and my shadow grows.</p>
</div>

Which properties to animate

For smooth, 60-frames-per-second animation, prefer **transform and opacity**. Animating width, height, top, left or margin forces the browser to recalculate the layout on every frame, which can stutter on phones.

Keyframe animations

Transitions animate between two states. Animations can run on their own, loop, and have many steps:

<style>
  @keyframes pulse {
    0%   { transform: scale(1); }
    50%  { transform: scale(1.08); }
    100% { transform: scale(1); }
  }
  @keyframes spin {
    to { transform: rotate(360deg); }
  }
  .live { display: inline-block; background: #ef4444; color: white; padding: 6px 14px; border-radius: 999px; animation: pulse 1.5s ease-in-out infinite; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .spinner { width: 32px; height: 32px; border: 4px solid #e2e8f0; border-top-color: #2563eb; border-radius: 50%; animation: spin 0.8s linear infinite; margin-top: 16px; }
</style>
<span class="live">● LIVE</span>
<div class="spinner" role="status" aria-label="Loading"></div>
  • @keyframes name { ... } defines the steps.
  • animation: name duration timing-function iteration-count; runs it.
  • infinite loops forever.

Respect reduced motion

Some people get dizzy or sick from movement on screen and turn on "reduce motion" in their system settings. Honour it:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

Good practice

  • Keep UI transitions short: 150–300ms. Longer feels slow.
  • Animate to give feedback (hover, open, close), not just for decoration.
  • Avoid things that flash more than three times a second.

Common mistakes

  • **Putting transition only on :hover**, so the change animates in but snaps back out.
  • Animating layout properties like width and top instead of transform.
  • **transition: all** catching unintended changes.
  • Endless decorative animations that distract from the content.

Exercise

  1. Give your buttons a 200ms colour transition on hover.
  2. Make cards lift with translateY and a bigger shadow on hover.
  3. Create a loading spinner with @keyframes.
  4. Add the reduced-motion media query to your stylesheet.

Summary

  • transition: property duration timing animates changes between states.
  • transform moves, scales and rotates without affecting layout.
  • Animate transform and opacity for smooth results.
  • @keyframes creates standalone animations; always respect prefers-reduced-motion.

Next, you'll learn CSS variables, which make large stylesheets easy to manage and theme.
